claim: 777 paired antibody profiles were analyzed, measured in 2010 (baseline) and 2014 (follow-up), measuring antibody responses to 21 A(H3N2) strains circulating over 47 years from a cohort in Guangzhou, China.
source: To test the hypothesis, we characterized the periodic behavior of 777 paired antibody profiles, measured in 2010 (baseline) and 2014 (follow-up), measuring antibody responses (i.e., hemagglutination inhibition [HI] titers) to 21 A(H3N2) strains circulating over 47 years (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3; Jiang et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of antibody profiles analyzed, the years of measurement, the number of strains tested, and the cohort location, with citations to prior work.

claim: Only 0.6% (n = 5) of participants self-reported influenza vaccinations between the two visits.
source: Only 0.6% (n = 5) of participants self-reported influenza vaccinations between the two visits; therefore, the observed changes in HI titers between the two visits were likely due to natural exposures.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific data on vaccination rates among participants.

claim: The observed changes in HI titers between the two visits were likely due to natural exposures.
source: Only 0.6% (n = 5) of participants self-reported influenza vaccinations between the two visits; therefore, the observed changes in HI titers between the two visits were likely due to natural exposures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low vaccination rate reported in the data.

claim: 33.6% (95% CI, 30.3–37.0%) of participants had a peak frequency corresponding to a long-term periodicity (i.e., 20–40 years) at baseline.
source: We found that 33.6% (95% CI, 30.3–37.0%) of participants had a peak frequency corresponding to a long-term periodicity (i.e., 20–40 years, translated from frequencies of 0.025–0.050; see 'Methods') at baseline, which was significantly higher than null expectation (Figure 1E), suggesting that the observed cyclic patterns were not purely due to chance.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific statistical results from Fourier analysis with confidence intervals.

claim: The proportion of participants with long-term periodicity at baseline was significantly higher than null expectation.
source: We found that 33.6% (95% CI, 30.3–37.0%) of participants had a peak frequency corresponding to a long-term periodicity (i.e., 20–40 years, translated from frequencies of 0.025–0.050; see 'Methods') at baseline, which was significantly higher than null expectation (Figure 1E), suggesting that the observed cyclic patterns were not purely due to chance.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding explicitly and references Figure 1E showing the comparison to permutations.

claim: The observed cyclic patterns were not purely due to chance.
source: We found that 33.6% (95% CI, 30.3–37.0%) of participants had a peak frequency corresponding to a long-term periodicity (i.e., 20–40 years, translated from frequencies of 0.025–0.050; see 'Methods') at baseline, which was significantly higher than null expectation (Figure 1E), suggesting that the observed cyclic patterns were not purely due to chance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical comparison to null expectation.

claim: The peak frequency range (corresponded to an ~24-year periodicity) accounted for a median 22.1% of the variance (interquartile range [IQR], 11.1–35.4%) of individual-level residuals.
source: This peak frequency range (corresponded to an ~24-year periodicity) accounted for a median 22.1% of the variance (interquartile range [IQR], 11.1–35.4%) of individual-level residuals (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical measures of variance explained by the identified periodicity.

claim: Similar periodicity was observed at follow-up.
source: We observed similar periodicity at follow-up, indicating that such pattern was unlikely to be affected by recent exposures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references a figure showing follow-up data.

claim: The cyclic pattern was unlikely to be affected by recent exposures.
source: We observed similar periodicity at follow-up, indicating that such pattern was unlikely to be affected by recent exposures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of periodicity between baseline and follow-up.

claim: The observed cycles in individual-level antibody responses were robust to analytic methods and sampling methods.
source: Across these analyses, including methods that accounted for variation in each individual's spectra (Figure 2A), irregularity in isolation intervals of tested strains (Figure 2B), and secular trends in our time series (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we found consistent evidence for long-term periodicity in antibody responses.
evidence: The manuscript describes multiple sensitivity analyses and states the results were consistent.

claim: Results were robust to leaving specific strains out of the analysis.
source: Results were robust to leaving specific strains out of the analysis (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3) and method of interpolation (Figure 1—figure supplements 7 and 8).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this robustness check and references supporting figures.

claim: Results were robust to method of interpolation.
source: Results were robust to leaving specific strains out of the analysis (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3) and method of interpolation (Figure 1—figure supplements 7 and 8).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this robustness check and references supporting figures.

claim: An independent out-of-sample data set from Vietnam showed similar long-term periodicity.
source: Additionally, we analyzed an independent out-of-sample data set from Vietnam (HI titers of 57 strains for 69 participants measured annually, 2007–2012; Horby et al., 2012; Kucharski et al., 2018). Due to the lack of data on age, we compared long-term periodicity in HI titers and found a similar long-term periodicity in both studies (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), suggesting that similar cycling is likely present in other settings, even with population-level variations.
evidence: The manuscript describes analysis of an independent dataset and reports similar findings, with citations.

claim: Similar cycling is likely present in other settings, even with population-level variations.
source: Additionally, we analyzed an independent out-of-sample data set from Vietnam (HI titers of 57 strains for 69 participants measured annually, 2007–2012; Horby et al., 2012; Kucharski et al., 2018). Due to the lack of data on age, we compared long-term periodicity in HI titers and found a similar long-term periodicity in both studies (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), suggesting that similar cycling is likely present in other settings, even with population-level variations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of findings across two different populations.

claim: Individual-level cross-reaction between antigenically similar strains likely explains the reported cycle.
source: Simulations suggested that individual-level cross-reaction between antigenically similar strains likely explains the reported cycle.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from simulation studies described in the manuscript.

claim: The reported cycles are predictable at both individual and birth cohort level.
source: We showed that the reported cycles are predictable at both individual and birth cohort level and that cohorts show a diversity of phases of these cycles.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding from their predictive analysis.

claim: Cohorts show a diversity of phases of these cycles.
source: We showed that the reported cycles are predictable at both individual and birth cohort level and that cohorts show a diversity of phases of these cycles.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation about cohort-level variation.

claim: Phase of cycle was associated with the risk of seroconversion to circulating strains, after accounting for age and pre-existing titers of the circulating strains.
source: Phase of cycle was associated with the risk of seroconversion to circulating strains, after accounting for age and pre-existing titers of the circulating strains.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding from their statistical analysis.

claim: Individuals who were predicted to be in phase IV were 14% (95% CI, 4–26%) more likely to experience seroconversion to the two recent strains compared to those in phase I.
source: We found that individuals who were predicted to be in phase IV (i.e., the last quarter of a cycle) were 14% (95% CI, 4–26%) more likely to experience seroconversion to the two recent strains compared to those in phase I (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical results from logistic regression analysis.

claim: There was high consistency between predicted and observed phases in 2012 across participants.
source: We found high consistency between predicted and observed phases in 2012 across participants (Figure 4C). For example, a consistency of 73% (95% CI, 65–79%) among individuals whose antibody responses were predicted to be in phase I (i.e., the first quarter of a cycle).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific statistical measures of prediction accuracy.

claim: A consistency of 73% (95% CI, 65–79%) was found among individuals whose antibody responses were predicted to be in phase I.
source: We found high consistency between predicted and observed phases in 2012 across participants (Figure 4C). For example, a consistency of 73% (95% CI, 65–79%) among individuals whose antibody responses were predicted to be in phase I (i.e., the first quarter of a cycle).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical results for prediction accuracy.

claim: The birth cohorts of 1986–90 had a higher proportion of participants in phase IV (55%, 95% CI, 39–70%) compared to 1961–65 (17%, 95% CI, 11–25%).
source: For example, we observed a higher proportion of participants who were in phase IV for the 2012 strain at baseline, when comparing the birth cohorts of 1986–90 (55%, 95% CI, 39–70%) with 1961–65 (17%, 95% CI, 11–25%; chi-squared test, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical comparisons between birth cohorts.

claim: Cohort-specific differences in phase composition correlated with the predicted cohort-specific composition of phase IV in 2012 (Pearson correlation = 0.67, p=0.01).
source: Moreover, we found that such cohort-specific differences in phase composition (Pearson correlation = 0.67, p=0.01; Figure 4F) and the resulting proportions of seroconversion (Pearson correlation = 0.63, p=0.02; Figure 4G) correlated with the predicted cohort-specific composition of phase IV in 2012.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific correlation statistics.

claim: The resulting proportions of seroconversion correlated with the predicted cohort-specific composition of phase IV in 2012 (Pearson correlation = 0.63, p=0.02).
source: Moreover, we found that such cohort-specific differences in phase composition (Pearson correlation = 0.67, p=0.01; Figure 4F) and the resulting proportions of seroconversion (Pearson correlation = 0.63, p=0.02; Figure 4G) correlated with the predicted cohort-specific composition of phase IV in 2012.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific correlation statistics.

claim: Such correlations disappeared when assuming a 35- or 6-year periodicity.
source: Such correlations disappeared when assuming a 35- or 6-year periodicity (i.e., periodicities that were not supported by observations in Figure 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from sensitivity analyses testing different periodicities.

claim: A diversity of phases was exhibited by members of the same age cohorts.
source: Of note, we found that a diversity of phases was exhibited by members of the same age cohorts, suggesting that individual's cycles could depart from other members of their birth cohort.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation about within-cohort variation.

claim: Individual's cycles could depart from other members of their birth cohort.
source: Of note, we found that a diversity of phases was exhibited by members of the same age cohorts, suggesting that individual's cycles could depart from other members of their birth cohort.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed diversity of phases within cohorts.

claim: Human antibody responses to influenza A(H3N2) display long-term periodicity.
source: We demonstrate that human antibody responses to influenza A(H3N2) display long-term periodicity, which are biologically consistent with nonlinear human adaptive immune responses (i.e., cross-reactions) to evolving viruses.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion in the Discussion section, summarizing the findings.

claim: The long-term periodicity is biologically consistent with nonlinear human adaptive immune responses (i.e., cross-reactions) to evolving viruses.
source: We demonstrate that human antibody responses to influenza A(H3N2) display long-term periodicity, which are biologically consistent with nonlinear human adaptive immune responses (i.e., cross-reactions) to evolving viruses.
evidence: This is an inference based on simulation results and biological knowledge.

claim: The observations are validated by different analytic methods and validation in a separate study population tested by a different antibody assay.
source: Our observations are validated by different analytic methods and validation in a separate study population tested by a different antibody assay.
evidence: The manuscript describes multiple validation approaches including the Vietnam cohort.

claim: The findings were robust to sampling and interpolation methods.
source: Our findings were robust to our sampling and interpolation methods.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on sensitivity analyses.

claim: At both individual and birth cohort levels, the phases of the antibody responses to the currently circulating strains are predictable and associated with seroconversion to these strains independent from the preexisting titers and age.
source: We further demonstrate that, at both individual and birth cohort levels, the phases of the antibody responses to the currently circulating strains are predictable and associated with seroconversion to these strains independent from the preexisting titers and age.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding, based on statistical analyses that controlled for these variables.

claim: The long-term periodicity was recovered only when including cross-reactions between antigenically similar strains in the simulations.
source: We were able to qualitatively recover the observed long-term periodicity only when including cross-reactions between antigenically similar strains in the simulations.
evidence: The manuscript describes simulation results showing this requirement.

claim: Model including repeated exposures or population-level A(H3N2) activity alone did not recover the long-term periodicity.
source: Particularly, our simulation results suggested that model including repeated exposures or population-level A(H3N2) activity alone did not recover the long-term periodicity (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific simulation results showing this negative finding.

claim: Strain-transcending antibody responses to past infections accumulate and build up contemporary antibody profiles.
source: Such findings fit in previous observations that strain-transcending antibody responses to past infections accumulate and build up contemporary antibody profiles (Fonville et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as consistent with prior literature, with citations provided.

claim: The long-term periodicity is a retrospective characterization of individual antibody profiles that arose from multiple exposures and cross-protection.
source: Of note, the long-term periodicity is a retrospective characterization of individual antibody profiles that arose from multiple exposures and cross-protection, which should not be directly interpreted as the duration of onward protection conferred by existing antibodies.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement clarifying what the periodicity represents.

claim: The long-term periodicity should not be directly interpreted as the duration of onward protection conferred by existing antibodies.
source: Of note, the long-term periodicity is a retrospective characterization of individual antibody profiles that arose from multiple exposures and cross-protection, which should not be directly interpreted as the duration of onward protection conferred by existing antibodies.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about interpretation of the findings.

claim: Within-subtype cross-reactions may drive individual-level long-term periodicity in antibody responses through temporal (but waning) cross-protection (i.e., positive feedback) and blunting generation of specific antibodies (i.e., negative feedback) against the circulating strains.
source: Within-subtype cross-reactions may drive individual-level long-term periodicity in antibody responses through temporal (but waning) cross-protection (i.e., positive feedback) and blunting generation of specific antibodies (i.e., negative feedback) against the circulating strains.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed based on the findings.

claim: A recent cohort study found that homotypic cross-protection against PCR-confirmed infections for up to five seasons after infections supported cross-protection that eventually wanes.
source: A recent cohort study found that homotypic cross-protection against PCR-confirmed infections for up to five seasons after infections supported cross-protection that eventually wanes (Wraith et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work supporting the proposed mechanism.

claim: The ~24-year periodicity implicitly suggested that antibodies gained from last immunizing events may interfere with the antibodies against the circulating strains for a maximum of 18 years.
source: In addition, the ~24-year periodicity implicitly suggested that antibodies gained from last immunizing events may interfere with the antibodies against the circulating strains for a maximum of 18 years (i.e., phases I–III in Figure 4B), before the antigenicity between the last immune strain and the circulating strain was too different to cause high-level cross-reactions in binding antibodies.
evidence: This is an inference about the duration of interference based on the observed periodicity.

claim: People's sera showed very little to no cross-reaction with strains that were isolated 20 years prior to their births.
source: This is in line with our previous findings that people's sera showed very little to no cross-reaction with strains that were isolated 20 years prior to their births (Lessler et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work by the authors supporting the interpretation.

claim: Long-term periodicity in HI titer may be driven by broad cross-reactions between strains that accumulate as people are exposed to multiple viruses over their lives.
source: Our findings suggest that long-term periodicity in HI titer may be driven by broad cross-reactions between strains that accumulate as people are exposed to multiple viruses over their lives.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the simulation results.

claim: The breadth of cross-reactions was determined by previously reported antigenic evolution.
source: The breadth of such cross-reactions was determined by previously reported antigenic evolution (Fonville et al., 2014; Kucharski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a parameter choice based on prior literature, with citations.

claim: Antigenic evolution rates significantly change the periodicity in individual antibody responses.
source: In simulations, we found that antigenic evolution rates significantly change the periodicity in individual antibody responses (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports simulation results showing this relationship.

claim: Slower antigenic evolution rates shift cycles in individual antibody responses to longer periodicity.
source: Slower antigenic evolution rates shift cycles in individual antibody responses to longer periodicity, with the extreme that people could acquire lifelong immunity against antigenically stable viruses (e.g., measles) (Amanna et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a simulation finding with a citation to support the extreme case.

claim: High rates of antigenic evolution could diminish the periodicity in antibody responses through frequent reactions to re-exposures.
source: Though in our simulations faster antigenic evolution led to shorter cycles, high rates of antigenic evolution could diminish the periodicity in antibody responses through frequent reactions to re-exposures.
evidence: This is stated as a simulation finding and interpretation.

claim: Associations were found between the phase of antibody response cycles and the risk of seroconversion to circulating strains after accounting for the homologous preexisting HI titers.
source: We found associations between the phase of antibody response cycles and the risk of seroconversion to circulating strains after accounting for the homologous preexisting HI titers.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from statistical analysis.

claim: The observed seroconversions likely reflected antibody responses after natural exposures during the study period due to low influenza vaccine coverage.
source: Due to the low influenza vaccine coverage in our participants and in China in general, the observed seroconversions likely reflected antibody responses after natural exposures during the study period.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low vaccination rate in the population.

claim: Previous studies have reported differential risk in individuals with the same homologous HI titer, proposing that unknown individual exposure histories and cohort effects are possible explanations.
source: Previous studies have reported differential risk in individuals with the same homologous HI titer, proposing that unknown individual exposure histories and cohort effects are possible explanations (Turbelin et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a citation to prior literature describing a known phenomenon.

claim: Cyclic patterns in an individual's antibody responses, which may be predictable at both individual and cohort levels, may contribute to heterogeneity in infection risk.
source: Our findings suggest that cyclic patterns in an individual's antibody responses, which may be predictable at both individual and cohort levels, may contribute to this heterogeneity.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings in relation to prior literature.

claim: Measuring seroconversion against a circulating strain could reveal a limited amount about protective immunity.
source: In addition, our findings suggested that measuring seroconversion against a circulating strain could reveal a limited amount about protective immunity.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the findings.

claim: Measuring responses to both circulating and previously circulating viruses (as well as calculating phase) could improve characterization of people's risk.
source: Measuring responses to both circulating and previously circulating viruses (as well as calculating phase) could improve characterization of people's risk (Quandelacy et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation based on the findings, with a citation.

claim: Resonance of cycles in individual-level antibody responses could form variations in phase distribution of antibody responses across birth cohorts.
source: We demonstrate that resonance of cycles in individual-level antibody responses could form variations in phase distribution of antibody responses across birth cohorts, which is consistent with previous findings that the fraction of A(H3N2) associated cases across different birth cohorts was found to change year to year (Turbelin et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding consistent with prior literature, with citations.

claim: The phase distribution of antibody responses across birth cohorts may be predictable and could be further used to predict the cohort-specific seroconversion against the circulating strains.
source: Our results also showed that the phase distribution of antibody responses across birth cohorts may be predictable and could be further used to predict the cohort-specific seroconversion against the circulating strains.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with potential application.

claim: This is potentially useful to determine and vaccinate the high-risk groups based on the exposure histories that could be shared by birth cohort.
source: This is potentially useful to determine and vaccinate the high-risk groups based on the exposure histories that could be shared by birth cohort.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the findings.

claim: Antigens with faster antigenic evolutions may attack different age groups at relatively similar risks, while antigens with slower antigenic evolutions tended to attack the children.
source: We did not attempt to explore the impact of antigenic evolution speed and the associated dynamics in antibody responses on shaping age-specific patterns of cases, while we speculate that antigens with faster antigenic evolutions may attack different age groups at relatively similar risks, while antigens with slower antigenic evolutions tended to attack the children (e.g., A(H3N2) vs. B/Victoria in Turbelin et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as speculation with reference to prior literature.

claim: Population-level virus activity alone was not able to recover the observed periodicity.
source: Simulation results further suggested that the population-level virus activity alone was not able to recover the observed periodicity, though epidemics with less regularity seemed to increase the variability in individual-level periodicity in the presence of broad cross-reactions (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The manuscript reports simulation results showing this finding.

claim: Epidemics with less regularity seemed to increase the variability in individual-level periodicity in the presence of broad cross-reactions.
source: Simulation results further suggested that the population-level virus activity alone was not able to recover the observed periodicity, though epidemics with less regularity seemed to increase the variability in individual-level periodicity in the presence of broad cross-reactions (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The manuscript reports simulation results showing this finding.

claim: HA-binding antibodies only mediate about half of the protection against influenza infections.
source: We recognize that HA-binding antibodies only mediate about half of the protection against influenza infections, while other forms of immunity, including neutralizing antibodies, non-HA head-specific inhibitory antibodies, and cellular immunity, would provide independent protections against infection and the severity of the diseases (Cowling et al., 2019; Meade et al., 2020; Ng et al., 2019; Stadlbauer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation with citations to supporting literature.

source: It is arguable that whether infections with A(H1N1) could confer years-long cross-protections against A(H3N2) in humans at individual level (Sonoguchi et al., 1985), while prior findings tended to support that between-subtype interaction could alter the transient cycles (i.e., within seasons) (Goldstein et al., 2011; Meade et al., 2020; Ranjeva et al., 2019).

claim: Only including population-level circulation could not recover the observed long-term periodicities in individual antibody responses.
source: Nevertheless, our simulation results suggested that only including population-level circulation – regardless of its underlying drivers – could not recover the observed long-term periodicities in individual antibody responses.
evidence: The manuscript reports simulation results showing this finding.

source: Second, our simulation results, while robust across parameter settings, may depend on the simplifying assumptions on immunological mechanisms we made (e.g., individual immunity-dependent protection) and therefore only qualitatively recovered the observed pattern.

source: Participants, aged 2–86 years old with a male-to-female ratio of 1.106:1 at baseline sampling, were recruited from households that were randomly selected in these locations.

claim: Three subtypes of influenza (A(H3N2), A(H1N1), and B) cause an estimated 291,000–645,000 deaths globally every year.
source: Three subtypes of influenza (A(H3N2), A(H1N1), and B) cause an estimated 291,000–645,000 deaths globally every year (Iuliano et al., 2018).

source: Although viruses of the same subtype share similar surface proteins, continuous genetic mutation leads to antigenic variation, resulting in escape from immune recognition by antibodies generated by previous infections.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about influenza evolution.

claim: Escape is not complete and cross-reactive immunity across strains exists for viruses isolated at different times.
source: However, escape is not complete. Cross-reactive immunity across strains exists for viruses isolated at different times (Bedford et al., 2014; Fonville et al., 2014; Krammer, 2019; Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to supporting literature.

source: Antibody-mediated immune response to multiple infections generated through repeated exposures to antigenically variable pathogens results in not only the facilitative interactions (e.g., back-boosting and cross-protection; Krammer, 2019), but also competitive interactions (e.g., immune imprinting; Gostic et al., 2016; Reynolds et al., 2022; Vieira et al., 2021), and antigenic seniority (Lessler et al., 2012).

claim: Antibody-mediated immune response to multiple infections generated through repeated exposures to antigenically variable pathogens results in competitive interactions (e.g., immune imprinting).
source: Antibody-mediated immune response to multiple infections generated through repeated exposures to antigenically variable pathogens results in not only the facilitative interactions (e.g., back-boosting and cross-protection; Krammer, 2019), but also competitive interactions (e.g., immune imprinting; Gostic et al., 2016; Reynolds et al., 2022; Vieira et al., 2021), and antigenic seniority (Lessler et al., 2012).

claim: Antibody-mediated immune response to multiple infections generated through repeated exposures to antigenically variable pathogens results in antigenic seniority.
source: Antibody-mediated immune response to multiple infections generated through repeated exposures to antigenically variable pathogens results in not only the facilitative interactions (e.g., back-boosting and cross-protection; Krammer, 2019), but also competitive interactions (e.g., immune imprinting; Gostic et al., 2016; Reynolds et al., 2022; Vieira et al., 2021), and antigenic seniority (Lessler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Antibodies mounted against a specific influenza virus decay (in either absolute magnitude or antigenic relevance) after exposure until re-exposure or infection to an antigenically similar virus occurs.
source: Antibodies mounted against a specific influenza virus decay (in either absolute magnitude or antigenic relevance) after exposure until re-exposure or infection to an antigenically similar virus occurs, whereupon back-boosting of antibodies acquired from previous infections (e.g., activation of memory B cells) can occur, as well as updating antigen-specific antibodies to the newly encountered infection (e.g., activation of naïve B cells) (Amanna et al., 2007; Edridge et al., 2020; Fonville et al., 2014; Kucharski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to supporting literature.
